headline: High-risk data leakage and cascading error: TREK’s browser/MCP-enabled, secret-handling defaults can amplify unsafe outputs from the non-networked spring-integration-samples pair.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no I/O surfaces, so it cannot be directly hijacked. B uses browsers and MCP by default, and its collaborative real-time tool use can ingest external content. The pairwise risk is that B may consume content originating from A-like outputs or shared artifacts without provenance checks; uncertainty remains because A’s ingestion path is undocumented, so I escalate from low to medium.
conditions: IF B ingests content from shared files, MCP tools, or browser pages without provenance checks, prompt injection is plausible.
IF A is wrapped by an orchestrator that forwards its text into B, the attack surface increases.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of untrusted text into B's MCP/browser workflows.
Add a provenance label to any A-generated artifact before B reads it.
Require manual review before B executes instructions found in files or web pages.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the handoff boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A is network-egress none, but B touches secrets, reservations, documents, photos, and logs, and can egress over allowlisted network paths. If A and B share a workspace or files, B can exfiltrate sensitive travel data to third parties through its APIs or browser flows. Because the shared-workspace assumption is not explicitly blocked, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF A and B share any filesystem, upload directory, or copied artifacts, B can read A-originated content and transmit it onward.
IF B is allowed to browse or call APIs on files containing secrets, leakage can occur through allowlisted egress.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces and separate OS users.
Remove B access to any directory containing A outputs.
Block B from handling files with secrets unless explicitly approved per run.
Rotate any exposed API keys or MFA secrets if shared artifacts were already exchanged.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention and egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or network surfaces, while B supports real-time collaborative sessions, multiple instances, files, and MCP/API calls. If both agents are pointed at the same mutable workspace or shared backend, B can overwrite or race on state that A also influences indirectly. The conflict is plausible in default collaborative deployments, but not proven from A alone, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or shared travel database, concurrent modification conflicts can occur.
IF B runs multiple instances against the same backend, race conditions become more likely.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate writable directory.
Serialize writes to any shared backend with a lock or queue.
Disable multi-instance writes for B during paired runs.
Review and reconcile file/database changes after each run.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control to shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B is a real-time collaborative travel planner with AI built in and can act on browser/API/MCP inputs; A is a separate sample repo with no runtime safeguards or verification path. If A-generated text is fed into B, B may treat it as authoritative and propagate errors into reservations, budgets, or documents. The downstream blast radius is multiple work products and potentially irreversible actions.
conditions: IF A output is used as an input source for B without verification, B can cascade errors into travel plans or reservations.
IF B is permitted to act on AI-generated facts, those facts can be rendered into user-visible or external actions.
mitigations: Require B to cite a source before acting on any A-derived claim.
Add a human approval step before reservations or budget changes.
Mark A outputs as untrusted drafts in B's UI.
Compare A-derived facts against a second source before use.
requires-engineering: implement verification gates for all downstream actions.

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles sensitive classes including email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while A is an open-source sample with no stated compliance controls. If the pair is deployed together and data from B is routed into A-derived tooling or logs, retention and residency obligations can diverge. A is not cited for compliance because it exposes no relevant controls; B alone drives the risk.
conditions: IF B stores secrets or personal travel data in logs or uploads that are later copied into A-derived tooling, compliance gaps can arise.
IF the deployment requires GDPR-style deletion or retention limits, B's file/log surfaces must honor them.
mitigations: Purge logs and uploads containing secrets after each run.
Restrict B from storing API keys or MFA secrets in plain files.
Document retention periods for travel.db, uploads, and trek.log.
Verify residency and DPA requirements before syncing data across systems.
requires-engineering: add automated retention and deletion controls.
